title: Dosas, Biryani, and Bhangra: Toronto's Massive South Asian Street Festival Returns This Weekend
excerpt: The 24th TD Festival of South Asia transforms Toronto's Little India into a two-day celebration of food, music, and diaspora community — and it is free.
body:
Toronto's Gerrard India Bazaar will shut down to traffic this weekend for one of North America's largest and most enduring South Asian cultural events. The 24th TD Festival of South Asia runs July 11 and 12, turning several blocks of Gerrard Street East into an open-air carnival of food, live performance, and community that draws tens of thousands of visitors each year.

Admission is free. Doors open at noon and the festivities run until 11 p.m. both days.

## The Food Trail

For the food-motivated — and that is most of the crowd — the festival's sprawling food trail is the main event. Vendors and local restaurants line the street with offerings that span the full breadth of South Asian cuisine: dosas from Tamil Nadu, biryani from Hyderabad, kebabs from Lucknow, chaats from Delhi, kulfi from Punjab, paan from Varanasi, and sugar cane juice from everywhere.

Gerrard India Bazaar, often called Toronto's Little India, is already one of the city's most concentrated corridors of South Asian food. During the festival weekend, that density multiplies. Visitors can hopscotch from a tandoor-fired naan stall to a Bengali mishti counter to a Sri Lankan kottu vendor without walking more than a few blocks.

The food is not exclusively Indian, either. The festival's South Asian umbrella encompasses Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Nepali, and Sri Lankan cuisines — reflecting the diversity of Toronto's South Asian community, one of the largest outside the subcontinent.

## Three Stages, 300-Plus Performers

The entertainment programming is equally expansive. More than 300 artists and performers are scheduled across three dynamic stages, with genres ranging from Bollywood and Bhangra to Qawwali, classical Bharatanatyam, Garba, folk, and contemporary fusion.

New this year is a dedicated Bangladesh Pavilion celebrating Bangladeshi culture, heritage, food, and performances. An "Impromptu Stage" will also give emerging artists a platform to perform live and connect with audiences — a nod to the festival's roots as a community-driven celebration rather than a corporate production.

Interactive dance workshops invite visitors to stop watching and start moving. A cultural wellness space offers yoga, henna, and guided meditation. And a Heritage Toronto activation booth provides guided walking tours through Gerrard India Bazaar, tracing the neighbourhood's history as a landing strip for South Asian immigrants who arrived in the 1970s and built a commercial district that still anchors the community.

## A Diaspora Institution at 24

The Festival of South Asia began in 2003 as a modest street fair organised by the Gerrard India Bazaar Business Improvement Area. Over nearly a quarter century, it has grown into a genuine diaspora institution — one of those rare events where second-generation kids, newly arrived immigrants, and non-South Asian Torontonians all show up and eat the same chaat.

Its longevity is worth noting in an era when diaspora cultural events tend to either corporatise beyond recognition or fizzle out after a few editions. The Festival of South Asia has done neither. It remains free, neighbourhood-anchored, and powered largely by local businesses and community organisations, with TD Bank as its title sponsor.

For NRIs across North America, the festival is a reminder that diaspora food culture does not have to live only in home kitchens or upscale restaurant tasting menus. Sometimes it is best experienced the way it was always meant to be: on a crowded street, standing up, with sauce dripping down your wrist and a Bhangra beat rattling your chest.

## If You Go

The 24th TD Festival of South Asia takes place July 11 and 12, 2026, from noon to 11 p.m., along Gerrard Street East between Glenside Avenue and Coxwell Avenue in Toronto. Admission is free. The nearest TTC access is the 506 College streetcar (get off at Gerrard/Ashdale) or Bus 22 from Coxwell Station. Gerrard Street East will be closed to vehicular traffic from Saturday morning through early Monday.

Insider tip: arrive before 2 p.m. if you want browsing room at the food stalls and vendor market. The evening crowds are formidable.
